# The problem

Under left truncation, subject $i$ enters at time $L_i > 0$ and appears in the
data only because they were still event-free at $L_i$. Anyone who failed before
they could enrol is never seen.

Every estimator in a survival forest — the splitting rule, the survival curve
in each leaf, and every metric used to score the fit — ultimately asks the same
question: **who is at risk at time $t$?** Standard software answers

$$R(t) = \{\, i : T_i \ge t \,\}$$

which assumes everyone was under observation from time zero. The correct answer
under delayed entry is

$$R_L(t) = \{\, i : L_i < t \le T_i \,\}$$

<div class="boxed">
**The whole project is this one substitution, applied consistently** — in the
splitting rule, in the leaf estimator, and in each evaluation metric.
</div>

Including a subject before $L_i$ biases results in a known direction: that
subject is *certain* to be event-free at $t$ by construction, not by prognosis.
This is the familiar immortal-time bias.

---

# Change 1 — The forest itself

### The leaf estimator

Each terminal node summarises its own subjects through one quantity — the
proportion failing at each event time $t_j$ in that node,

$$\frac{d_j}{n_j}, \qquad d_j = \text{events at } t_j, \quad n_j = \bigl|R(t_j)\bigr|$$

from which the node reports both of the usual estimators:

$$\hat{H}(t) = \sum_{t_j \le t} \frac{d_j}{n_j}
\qquad\text{(Nelson–Aalen, cumulative hazard)}$$

$$\hat{S}(t) = \prod_{t_j \le t}\left(1 - \frac{d_j}{n_j}\right)
\qquad\text{(Kaplan–Meier, survival)}$$

The correction replaces $n_j = |R(t_j)|$ with $n_j = |R_L(t_j)|$. **Only that
denominator changes.**

Because both estimators are built from the same ratio $d_j / n_j$, this single
substitution corrects the hazard and the survival curve at once — and
everything downstream of them inherits it.

### The splitting rule

A split is chosen by the log-rank statistic comparing daughter nodes. Its
observed-minus-expected term,

$$O - E \;=\; \sum_j \left( d_{1j} - d_j\,\frac{n_{1j}}{n_j} \right),$$

depends on the at-risk counts $n_{1j}, n_j$ at each event time. Those counts are
now taken over $R_L(t_j)$ rather than $R(t_j)$.

### The check that this is correct

Setting $L_i = 0$ for all $i$ gives $R_L(t) = R(t)$
identically, so the entry-aware forest must reproduce the standard forest
*exactly*. Computed live:

```{r noop}
set.seed(2024); n <- 250
dd <- data.frame(x1 = rnorm(n), x2 = rnorm(n), x3 = rnorm(n))
dd$time <- rexp(n, rate = 0.2 * exp(dd$x1)); dd$status <- rbinom(n, 1, .75)
a <- rfsrc(Surv(time, status) ~ ., dd, ntree = 100, seed = -11)
b <- rfsrc(Surv(time, status) ~ ., dd, ntree = 100, seed = -11, entry.time = rep(0, n))
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Quantity = c("survival $\\hat S(t\\mid x)$", "cumulative hazard $\\hat H(t\\mid x)$",
               "out-of-bag error", "tree sizes"),
  `Maximum absolute difference` = c(
    max(abs(a$survival.oob - b$survival.oob), na.rm = TRUE),
    max(abs(a$chf.oob - b$chf.oob), na.rm = TRUE),
    max(abs(a$err.rate - b$err.rate), na.rm = TRUE),
    max(abs(a$leaf.count - b$leaf.count))),
  check.names = FALSE), align = "lr")
```

Exactly zero. This is re-checked on every replication of every simulation and
has held every time.

---

# Change 2 — The evaluation metrics

A metric needs correcting only if it **compares subjects against one another at
a point in time**. That is where an unadjusted metric can compare subject $i$'s
outcome against a subject $j$ who had not yet entered the study. Metrics that
look only at one subject's own predicted curve, or at tree structure, are
unaffected.

Three metrics needed it.

## C-index

Measures whether the subject who failed first was predicted to be riskier. It
averages over *comparable pairs*. A pair $(i,j)$ is comparable when

$$\delta_i = 1, \qquad T_i < T_j$$

Under delayed entry we require in addition that $j$ was actually under
observation when $i$ failed:

$$\delta_i = 1, \qquad T_i < T_j, \qquad \underbrace{L_j \le T_i}_{\text{added}}$$

Without the third condition the model is credited for correctly ranking a
subject who could not have failed at that time, because they had not yet
enrolled.

## Brier score

Measures calibration at a fixed $t$: the squared distance between the predicted
probability and what happened. With $Y_i(t) = I(T_i > t)$,

$$\mathrm{BS}(t) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i(t)\,
\bigl[\,Y_i(t) - \hat S(t \mid X_i)\,\bigr]^2$$

Three changes, each with a distinct role:

**(a) Restrict the sample.** Average over $R_L(t)$, not all $N$:

$$\mathrm{BS}_L(t) = \frac{1}{|R_L(t)|}\sum_{i \in R_L(t)} \cdots$$

**(b) Condition the prediction.** A subject under observation has already
survived to $L_i$, so the relevant probability is conditional:

$$\hat S(t \mid X_i) \;\longrightarrow\; \frac{\hat S(t \mid X_i)}{\hat S(L_i \mid X_i)}$$

**(c) Reweight.** Alongside the usual inverse-probability-of-censoring weight
$1/G_C$, an inverse-probability-of-truncation weight $1/G_L$, where
$G_L(t) = P(L \le t)$ is the entry-time distribution:

$$w_i(t) = \frac{1}{G_C(\cdot)}\;\longrightarrow\;\frac{1}{G_C(\cdot)\,G_L(\cdot)}$$

CRPS is $\mathrm{BS}_L(t)$ integrated over $t$.

## Time-dependent AUC

At each $t$ the sample splits into **cases** (failed by $t$) and **controls**
(still event-free), and we ask how often a case is ranked riskier:

$$\text{Cases}(t) = \{i : T_i \le t,\ \delta_i = 1\}, \qquad
\text{Controls}(t) = \{j : T_j > t\}$$

$$\mathrm{AUC}(t) = P\bigl(M_i(t) > M_j(t) \;\bigm|\; i \in \text{Cases}(t),\, j \in \text{Controls}(t)\bigr)$$

with marker $M_i(t) = 1 - \hat S(t \mid X_i)$. The same three changes apply —
restrict both sets to $\{L \le t\}$, condition the marker on survival to $L_i$,
and add the truncation weight.

> **One clean consequence.** For a case, $L_i \le T_i \le t$ holds
> automatically, so $\text{Cases}_L(t) = \text{Cases}(t)$ — the restriction
> **only ever removes controls**. This pins the direction of the bias: an
> unadjusted AUC inflates the control pool with subjects guaranteed to be
> event-free at $t$ by construction.

### Why add this when we already have the C-index

The C-index collapses every comparable pair into one number. The AUC asks the
same question *separately at each $t$*, against the risk set alive then — and
that is precisely what left truncation distorts. It tests something the
C-index structurally cannot.

---

# What the simulations show

Six data-generating processes: two where Cox is exactly correct, four
violating proportional hazards in different ways. Each fits the **same** model
twice on the **same** sample:

- **Phase 1** — the model is given $L_i = 0$ for everyone.
- **Phase 2** — the model is given the true $L_i$.

Since Phase 1 provably equals the standard model (the zero check above), this
is a clean paired comparison isolating one thing: the value of knowing the
entry time.

```{r results}
sims <- c("01_cox_random_forerst_lt","02_flexihaz_gompertz_lt","03_rist_scenario1_lt",
          "04_rist_scenario2_lt","05_rist_scenario3_lt","06_rist_scenario4_lt")
lab <- c("Cox PH (Cox correct)","Gompertz (PH violated)","RIST 1 (Cox correct)",
         "RIST 2 (nonlinear)","RIST 3 (Gamma, PH violated)","RIST 4 (Lognormal, PH violated)")
p <- file.path("..","simulations",sims,"results_phases.rds")
if (all(file.exists(p))) {
  rl <- lapply(p, readRDS); nrep <- unique(sapply(rl, function(r) r$n_rep))
  pick <- function(r,f,fam){m<-colMeans(r[[f]])
    sprintf("%+.1f%%",(m[[paste0("p1_",fam,"_lt")]]-m[[paste0("p2_",fam,"_lt")]])/m[[paste0("p1_",fam,"_lt")]]*100)}
  have <- c(overall="MAD",cindex="C-index",brier="Brier",auc="AUC")
  have <- have[sapply(names(have),function(f) all(sapply(rl,function(r) !is.null(r[[f]]))))]
  tb <- data.frame(DGP=lab, check.names=FALSE)
  for (f in names(have)) for (fam in c("cox","rsf"))
    tb[[paste(have[[f]], toupper(fam))]] <- sapply(rl,pick,f=f,fam=fam)
  knitr::kable(tb, align=c("l",rep("r",ncol(tb)-1)))
} else { nrep <- NA; cat("_(results not available)_") }
```

Each cell is the **percentage reduction in error** from supplying the true
entry times. All four metrics are placed on an error scale first (the two
ranking metrics enter as $1-C$ and $1-\mathrm{AUC}$), so **positive means the
entry time helped**, for every column alike.

```{r caveat, results='asis'}
if (!is.na(nrep[1]) && max(nrep) < 100)
  cat(sprintf("> **Provisional:** %s replications per simulation. Large effects are
> stable at this size; the near-zero C-index entries are not distinguishable
> from Monte Carlo error. The production run is 100 replications.\n",
paste(unique(nrep), collapse="/")))
```

### Reading the pattern

Knowing the entry time produces **large, consistent gains in the accuracy and
calibration of the estimated curves** (MAD, Brier) across every DGP, whether or
not proportional hazards holds. The gain in pure *ranking* (C-index) is near
zero.

That contrast is itself the substantive finding, and it is statistically
sensible: left truncation distorts the **level** of the survival curve far more
than it distorts the **ordering** of subjects. A biased risk set inflates
$\hat H$ at early times for everyone, which moves every curve in the same
direction — leaving relative ranks largely intact.

The time-dependent AUC was added to test that interpretation at each $t$ rather
than averaged over all of them.

---

# One open question

We assumed that scoring a model on a **held-out test set** would require
extending the software. On checking, it does not.

In a survival forest a test subject's predicted curve **is** the curve of the
leaf it falls into, and that curve is estimated entirely from *training* data.
The subject's own $L_i$ affects neither which leaf it reaches (determined by
covariates) nor the curve stored there. It affects only how we *score* the
prediction — and all three corrected metrics accept test-set entry times
already.

```{r predict}
set.seed(5)
mk <- function(np){X<-matrix(rnorm(np*3),np,3);colnames(X)<-paste0("x",1:3)
  Tt<-rexp(np,rate=.15*exp(X[,1]-.7*X[,2]));Cc<-rexp(np,rate=.08);L<-rexp(np,rate=.35)
  k<-L<pmin(Tt,Cc);data.frame(entry=L[k],time=pmin(Tt,Cc)[k],status=1*(Tt<=Cc)[k],X[k,,drop=FALSE])}
tr<-mk(900); te<-mk(600)
f<-rfsrc(Surv(time,status)~.,tr[,-1],ntree=200,entry.time=tr$entry,seed=-3)
pr<-predict(f,newdata=te[,-1])
o<-list(family="surv",yvar=cbind(te$time,te$status),predicted=rowSums(1-pr$survival),
        predicted.oob=rowSums(1-pr$survival),survival.oob=pr$survival,
        time.interest=f$time.interest,
        forest=list(yvar=cbind(te$time,te$status),xvar=data.frame(.d=rep(0,nrow(te)))),
        imputed.indv=NULL); class(o)<-c("rfsrc","grow","surv")
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  `Test-set metric`=c("C-index error","Brier (CRPS)","AUC"),
  `Ignoring entry times`=c(sprintf("%.3f",get.cindex(te$time,te$status,pr$predicted)),
     sprintf("%.3f",get.brier.survival(o,cens.model="km")$crps),
     sprintf("%.3f",get.auc.survival(o,cens.model="km")$iauc)),
  `Using entry times`=c(sprintf("%.3f",get.cindex(te$time,te$status,pr$predicted,entry=te$entry)),
     sprintf("%.3f",get.brier.survival(o,cens.model="km",entry.time=te$entry)$crps),
     sprintf("%.3f",get.auc.survival(o,cens.model="km",entry.time=te$entry)$iauc)),
  check.names=FALSE), align="lrr")
```

So held-out evaluation is already available. The single remaining gap is
**variable importance computed on a test set**, which is calculated internally
by the software and cannot reach the corrected metrics. Closing it is a
substantial piece of work on the underlying C code.

> **The question for discussion:** does the analysis need variable importance
> on held-out data? Importance on the training sample is available and now
> carries correct confidence intervals. If training-sample importance is
> sufficient, this item can be closed.

# Summary

```{r summary}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Component = c("Splitting rule", "Leaf survival estimator", "C-index",
                "Brier score / CRPS", "Time-dependent AUC",
                "Variable importance + confidence intervals",
                "Held-out (test-set) scoring",
                "Held-out variable importance"),
  Status = c("Done","Done","Done","Done","Done","Done","Available","Open — see above"),
  check.names = FALSE), align = "ll")
```

One limitation worth recording: the correction was made to the default
(log-rank) splitting rule. The package's alternative splitting rules do not
have it, so they should not be combined with entry times. All results here use
the default.

Full derivations for each metric are in the accompanying notes
(`c_index_left_truncation.md`, `brier_score_left_truncation.md`,
`auc_left_truncation.md`).
